title: FAR U3·W4 — Accounting Changes, Errors, Interim & Segment Reporting (CPA Core)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — restate, adjust, or just go forward?

When MBG changes how it accounts for something — or discovers a prior mistake — FAR prescribes exactly one of three treatments, and choosing the wrong one is a classic exam miss. The rule turns on whether it is a change in principle, a change in estimate, or an error. This week settles all three and adds interim and segment reporting.

The three treatments (ASC 250)

  • Change in accounting principle — switching from one acceptable GAAP method to another (e.g., FIFO to weighted-average inventory). Apply it retrospectively: restate prior periods presented and adjust the opening balance of retained earnings for the earliest period.
  • Change in accounting estimate — revising a judgment as new information arrives (useful life, salvage, bad-debt rate, warranty rate). Apply it prospectively: current and future periods only; do not touch prior periods.
  • Error correction — a mistake in previously issued statements (math error, misapplied GAAP, overlooked facts). Restate the prior periods (a prior-period adjustment to beginning retained earnings).

The depreciation-method trap

A change in depreciation method (say, double-declining-balance to straight-line) looks like a change in principle but is treated as a change in estimate effected by a change in principle — so it is accounted for prospectively, not retrospectively. This is one of FAR's favorite distractors: it is the prior estimate of how the asset is consumed that is changing.

A change in reporting entity (e.g., changing the entities in consolidated statements) is applied retrospectively, like a principle change.

Counterbalancing errors

Some errors counterbalance — they self-correct over two periods (e.g., an inventory misstatement reverses the next year). If found after two years and the books are closed, no entry is needed for the income effect, though prior-period statements presented still need correcting. Non-counterbalancing errors (e.g., a depreciation error) persist until fixed.

Interim and segment reporting

Interim reporting (ASC 270) generally treats each interim period as an integral part of the annual period: income taxes, for instance, use the estimated annual effective tax rate applied to year-to-date income. Segment reporting (ASC 280) uses the management approach — segments are reported the way management runs the business — and a segment is reportable if it meets any 10% threshold of total revenue, profit or loss, or assets, with reported segments covering at least 75% of external revenue.

Retrospective application and its limits

Applying a principle change retrospectively means restating each prior period presented as if the new method had always been used, and adjusting the opening retained earnings of the earliest period shown for the cumulative effect on still-earlier years. Only the direct effects (and related income-tax effects) are restated; indirect effects — such as a profit-sharing accrual that would have differed — are recognized in the period of change, not restated. When it is impracticable to determine the period-specific or cumulative effect (the data simply do not exist), the change is applied prospectively from the earliest practicable date — an explicit exception the exam tests against students who assume retrospective is always possible.

Disclosures and the justification requirement

A voluntary change in principle is permitted only if the new method is preferable, and management must justify that preferability — you cannot switch methods to smooth earnings at will. The change is disclosed with its nature and reason, the method of applying it, and the effect on income, per-share amounts, and affected line items for each period presented. A material change in estimate is disclosed as to its effect, and an error correction is disclosed as a restatement, including the nature of the error and the effect on each prior period and on opening retained earnings. This audit-trail discipline mirrors the integrity controls emphasized throughout the program.

Interim reporting — integral view and exceptions

Treating an interim period as an integral part of the year drives several rules. The estimated annual effective tax rate is re-estimated each quarter and applied year-to-date, so a later quarter catches up any change. Some costs that benefit the whole year may be allocated across interim periods. But several items are recognized discretely, in the period they occur: a permanent inventory write-down (a temporary market decline expected to reverse by year-end is not recognized), a loss contingency, and a LIFO liquidation expected to be replaced by year-end (interim cost of sales includes the expected replacement cost). Publicly traded companies present condensed interim statements under SEC rules, with minimum disclosures emphasizing seasonality and significant changes.

Segment reporting mechanics

Under the management approach, operating segments are the components whose results the chief operating decision maker reviews to allocate resources. A segment is reportable if it meets any one of three 10% tests: its revenue (including intersegment) is 10% or more of combined revenue; the absolute value of its profit or loss is 10% or more of the greater (in absolute value) of total segment profit or total segment loss; or its assets are 10% or more of combined segment assets. If the reportable segments’ combined external revenue is below 75% of consolidated revenue, add segments until the 75% threshold is met. Segments similar in economics and other factors may be aggregated.

A worked threshold and entity-wide disclosures

Worked test: total combined segment revenue is $10,000,000. A division with $1,300,000 of revenue clears the 10% revenue test ($1,300,000 > $1,000,000) and is reportable even if it runs at a loss, because any single 10% test suffices. Beyond segment detail, ASC 280 requires entity-wide disclosures regardless of segments: revenues from external customers by product or service and by geographic area (domestic versus foreign, with material individual countries), long-lived assets by geography, and the existence of any major customer providing 10% or more of total revenue (with the amount and segment, though the customer need not be named). These reveal the concentration information consolidated totals hide.

A worked counterbalancing error

Suppose ending inventory in Year 1 is understated by $30,000. Understated ending inventory overstates cost of goods sold and understates Year 1 net income by $30,000. Because Year 1 ending inventory is Year 2 beginning inventory, Year 2 cost of goods sold is understated and Year 2 net income is overstated by the same $30,000 — the error counterbalances, leaving retained earnings correct by the end of Year 2. If discovered during Year 2 before closing, correct both years; if discovered after Year 2 closes, retained earnings has already self-corrected and no income adjustment is needed, though any comparative statements still shown must be restated. A non-counterbalancing error — for example, capitalizing an item that should have been expensed — does not self-correct and must be fixed whenever found.

CMA bridge

CMA month 3 covered segment reporting for performance; FAR adds the ASC 280 quantitative thresholds and the management approach. The estimate-versus-principle distinction echoes the relevant-cost discipline — know precisely which rule applies before you compute.

Practice and recap

  1. Change in principle → retrospective; change in estimate → prospective; error → restate.
  2. A depreciation-method change is a change in estimate (prospective).
  3. Recognize counterbalancing errors that self-correct over two periods.
  4. Interim tax uses the estimated annual effective rate; segments use the management approach and 10% thresholds.

Recap: retrospective for principle and reporting-entity changes, prospective for estimates (including depreciation-method changes), and restatement for errors — while interim periods apply the estimated annual effective tax rate and segments follow the management approach with 10% reportability thresholds.

flashcards.back: Retrospective: restate prior periods and adjust opening retained earnings.
Prospective: current and future periods only.
Restate prior periods (prior-period adjustment to beginning retained earnings).
Change in estimate effected by a change in principle → prospective.
An error that self-corrects over two periods (e.g., an inventory misstatement reversing next year).
Use the estimated annual effective tax rate applied to year-to-date income.
Reportable if a segment meets any 10% test of revenue, profit/loss, or assets (management approach).

quiz.title: Accounting Changes, Errors, Interim and Segment

questions.q: A change from FIFO to weighted-average inventory is a change in:
questions.explain: A change in accounting principle is applied retrospectively.

questions.q: Revising the useful life of equipment is a change in:
questions.explain: A change in estimate is applied prospectively.

questions.q: A change in depreciation METHOD is accounted for:
choices: Prospectively as a change in estimate
questions.explain: It is a change in estimate effected by a change in principle — prospective.

questions.q: Discovering that a prior year's statements misapplied GAAP requires:
questions.explain: Errors in prior issued statements are corrected by restatement.

questions.q: For interim reporting, income tax is computed using the:
questions.explain: Interim tax applies the estimated annual effective rate to year-to-date income.

questions.q: An operating segment is reportable under ASC 280 if it meets a 10% threshold of:
choices: Revenue, profit or loss, or assets
questions.explain: Any 10% test of revenue, profit/loss, or assets makes a segment reportable.

questions.q: A change in the set of entities in consolidated statements (reporting entity) is applied:
questions.explain: A change in reporting entity is applied retrospectively.
